summary: A 1971 first cut at a proposed Telnet protocol, by J. T. Melvin and R. W. Watson. Telnet lets a user at one computer act as a terminal on another. It is an early proposal.

eli5.summary: A first draft of rules that let you sit at one computer and use another far away.

subtitle: An early sketch of Telnet, which lets a terminal at one site act like a terminal directly attached to a remote server.

tldr.problem: Users wanted interactive access over the ARPA Network to remote systems, starting with online access to the Network Information Center.
tldr.mechanism: A Telnet process at the user site makes the user's terminal appear logically equivalent to one directly connected to the server, with conventions for echoing, format characters and carriage return.
tldr.outcome: The authors expect the final Telnet protocol to differ, and leave several problems, such as line-at-a-time systems and interrupts, for further study.

today: RFC 97 is an early proposal whose own text says the final Telnet protocol will differ. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 97, by John T. Melvin and Richard W. Watson of SRI-ARC, dated 15 February 1971, describes Telnet: a process at a user's site that lets a typewriter-like terminal get interactive service from a remote server site over the ARPA Network. It was motivated by the need to set specifications for online access to the Network Information Center (NIC).

The authors say outright that other sites may find it hard to meet all the requirements, so the final protocol will differ from this one. They hope for an initial standard to be agreed quickly so that users can get onto the network.
sections.eli5: Two people sketch how to use a faraway computer from your own keyboard, and say it is only a first draft.

sections.title: Design Problems
sections.content:
The basic assumption is that the user's terminal should appear over the network as logically equivalent to a terminal directly connected to the server. That implies the user can generate all codes a server terminal can (for the NIC, all 128 ASCII codes), can escape back to the local system or from the server process, and that line-at-a-time and character-at-a-time Telnets can work with each other.

The paper lists three echo cases: character-at-a-time with the server echoing, character-at-a-time with the user site echoing, and line-at-a-time with the user site echoing. It also raises how to handle format characters (HT, VT, FF, LF, CR) and whether network message boundaries can stay invisible to user processes.
sections.eli5: The tricky part is that different computers type, echo and end lines in different ways, so the rules must make them all look alike.

sections.title: Proposed Conventions
sections.content:
The server site assumes at first that the user site does the echoing, until told otherwise. The server expects the same characters a directly connected terminal can generate, at least 128-character ASCII, and the user Telnet may need two-character sequences for upper and lower case and for control codes.

For the carriage return, a CR struck at the terminal gets sent as a CR over the network. If the user system turns it into CRLF or an end-of-line code, Telnet converts it back. When the user system echoes, it can default to echoing a CRLF on each CR received.

The paper also proposes a user-assignable end of stream (EOS) character, to separate end-of-stream as a network function from end-of-line as a system function. It warns that using INS control commands might introduce race conditions, and leaves line-at-a-time systems and interrupt or escape handling for further study.
sections.eli5: When you press Enter, the same signal should always go down the wire, and each end works out what it means on its own side.

sections.title: Appendix: Access to the NIC
sections.content:
Appendix A applies the conventions to the NLS(NIC) system. Connection setup reuses the steps in RFC 80, using the NIC logger at socket 1 and a pair of connections. The first 8 bits received are the message data type, 00000001, for an 8-bit ASCII stream as in RFC 63, and each network message holds a whole number of 8-bit units.

NCP-generated interrupts are disabled at the NIC. A user-definable ASCII code, presently DEL (ASCII '177), aborts the running process and returns to the main NLS(NIC) command processor. Echoing is assumed to be done by the user site unless the NIC is told otherwise.
sections.eli5: The last part gives the exact steps for calling one particular computer, the one that kept the network's documents.
